sections.h2: Finding the Midland County recording counter
sections.html:
The Register of Deeds sits at 220 W Ellsworth Street in Midland, MI 48640, and answers at (989) 832-6820. The counter takes new documents on weekdays from 8 a.m. until 4 p.m. The vault holding the older books opens thirty minutes after that.

Anything arriving after 4 p.m. waits for the next business day, and papers are worked in the order received, provided payment came with them. Counter staff record warranty and quit claim deeds, land contracts, releases, powers of attorney, liens and plats. They do not draft documents or advise on law, so an attorney or title company writes the deed.

Any document, short or long, is recorded for one $30.00 charge that already folds in the state remonumentation and automation charges. A few add-ons exist.

Midland County Register of Deeds fees
ServiceAmount
Recording one document$30.00
Document assigning or discharging more than one instrument$3.00 per instrument beyond the first, added to $30.00
Treasurer's tax certificate$5.00 covers up to 5 legal descriptions, then $1.00 each
Plain copy$1.00 per page
Certified copy$5.00 plus $1.00 per page

You can pay with cash, a check payable to the Register of Deeds, or a card at the counter, where the card processor adds a charge generally about $1.50. Qualified submitters may e-record, but a paper that needs a raised court seal or a death certificate must come in on paper.

sections.h2: Instruments held up without a treasurer's certificate
sections.html:
The treasurer must issue a certificate before any of these four can be recorded:

  • A warranty deed, or any deed that includes a covenant of warranty.
  • A land contract.
  • A land contract assignment containing a warranty clause.
  • A master deed for a site condominium project.

Get the certificate ordered before closing day. A plain quit claim deed needs none. To see whether a parcel's taxes are current, use the county's online lookup, which shows what the treasurer's counter would.

The county's chart shows $3.75 for the state and $0.55 for the county on each $500, so $4.30 together. At a $100,000 price the chart columns read $750, $110 and $860. Tax applies from $100 of value upward, subject to the exemption sheets the office links.

Buyer and seller can keep the price off the deed by attaching a Real Estate Transfer Tax Valuation Affidavit. A different form, the Property Transfer Affidavit, goes to the assessor for the City of Midland or for the township that holds the parcel, and state law allows the buyer 45 days.

Your title company usually runs these, but knowing the sequence shows a seller where the paper and the money travel.

  • Ask the treasurer for a tax certificate if the deed warrants title.
  • Sign before a notary. Register staff will not notarize, but the County Clerk in the same County Services Building offers it for a small fee.
  • Send the state and county transfer taxes to the county treasurer within 15 days of delivering the deed (MCL 207.523(3)).
  • File the deed with the $30.00 fee before the 4 p.m. cutoff.
  • The buyer then has 45 days to give the Property Transfer Affidavit to the City of Midland or township assessor.

Recorders also pass a list of recorded transactions to local assessors at least monthly under MCL 211.27a(10).

The oldest records date to 1855, the year the county was established. Books and microfilm cover the whole run, scanned images with computer indexing start in 1968, and online images reach back to 1950. Online searching uses Fidlar-hosted tools named Tapestry EON and Laredo. Recorded papers are public, and anyone may ask for copies.

The index for 1958 to 1968 is available in an Adobe search format, and entries older than 1958 turn up in the Simple Search option. Back-indexing is still underway, so an older chain of title may call for a visit or a phone call. The recording page also links a property fraud alert and a reporting form, worth using when an inherited parcel still carries a relative's name.

The county seat is Midland, and Coleman is the county's other incorporated city. The Tittabawassee River runs through Edenville Township and past the village of Sanford. In May 2020 the Edenville and Sanford dam failures forced evacuations across parts of the city, the village and several townships, so a seller near the river should expect buyers to ask about flood history.

Utilities differ from one parcel to the next. The city of Midland provides water and sewer to its residents and a few neighboring townships, while parcels beyond municipal water rely on private wells and septic systems. Out in the townships, collect well and septic records before listing.

The county held an estimated 83,754 people in July 2025, living among 37,723 housing units, and growth since 2020 has been slight. Owner-occupants hold 78.1 percent of homes, and the middle-priced owned house is valued at $195,400. Renters pay about $1,016 a month. With just 128 building permits issued in 2025, a resale listing faces little new-build competition.

Roughly nine in ten residents lived at the same address a year earlier, a sign of long tenure, so many sellers have held their homes for years and have old deeds and easements to dig out.

With turnover low, a house with clean, well-kept title records stands out. Having the deed, tax certificate and any well or septic records ready makes your listing easier to price and to close.

Round up your current deed, any older family deeds and the newest tax bill. If a mortgage is being paid off, expect a release to be recorded for a fee. Find out from the title company soon whether a treasurer's certificate is required, and confirm the closing date leaves time to reach the counter before 4 p.m. If a river-area home is involved, add any flood or insurance paperwork to the pile.

Expect to pay the $30.00 recording fee on the deed, plus the same fee for each release if a lender is being paid off. Keep receipts, because the county gives a plain copy for $1.00 a page if you need one later.

A cash sale avoids the lender's appraisal and underwriting wait. The deed still goes through the same notary, certificate and transfer tax steps.

If you do not yet have a deed drafted for the buyer, the register's staff cannot prepare one for you. Line up an attorney or the title company first. Once the deed is signed and notarized, pick a time of day well before the afternoon cutoff, because a late arrival simply rolls to the next business day and can push back your funding.

faqs.q: Where do I take a Midland deed, and until when?
faqs.a: 220 W Ellsworth Street, Midland, MI 48640, phone (989) 832-6820. Recording closes at 4 p.m. on weekdays, and papers received later are recorded the next business day.

faqs.q: What does it cost to file one deed?
faqs.a: One document costs $30.00, whatever its length. A treasurer's tax certificate for a warranty deed adds $5.00 for up to five legal descriptions.

faqs.q: Does Midland County take e-recorded deeds?
faqs.a: Yes, from qualified submitters, even when the document needs tax certification. Paper is still required for documents that need a raised court seal or a death certificate.

faqs.q: Will the counter staff notarize or draft my deed?
faqs.a: No. The office does not write legal documents, and its own staff do not notarize what they record. The County Clerk's office in the same building has a notary available for a small fee.
For each $500 of price the chart lists $3.75 for the state plus $0.55 for the county, or $4.30 together. The seller pays within 15 days after the deed is delivered, unless an exemption applies.
